prompt: In an older car without anti-lock brakes, your brake pedal suddenly sinks to the floor. What should you try first?
choices: Pump the brake pedal quickly several times
Turn the ignition off right away
Shift into Park
Hold the pedal on the floor and wait for the car to stop
explanation: Pumping the pedal fast and hard can build up enough brake pressure to stop the car. Turning the engine off or shifting to Park while moving can cost you steering control or damage the car.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 109, PA p. 67, MT p. 87)

prompt: Your brakes have failed and pumping the pedal does not help. What should you do next?
choices: Yank the parking brake on as hard as you can
Shift into Reverse to stop the wheels
Apply the parking brake gradually, ready to release it if the rear wheels lock
Turn the key to the Lock position
explanation: Use the parking (emergency) brake slowly and hold the release so you can ease off if the rear wheels lock and the car starts to skid. Pulling it hard all at once can lock the wheels.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 67, AZ p. 69, TX p. 55)

prompt: A front tire suddenly blows out at highway speed. What should you do first?
choices: Brake hard to stop quickly
Hold the steering wheel firmly with both hands
Steer sharply onto the shoulder
Shift into neutral
explanation: Grip the wheel firmly and keep the car going straight. Hard braking or sharp steering right after a blowout can make you skid or lose control.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 109, PA p. 67, AZ p. 68)

prompt: How should you slow down after a tire blowout?
choices: Take your foot off the gas and slam on the brakes
Shift into neutral and coast
Pull the parking brake
Gradually ease off the gas pedal and let the car slow down
explanation: Release the gas gradually while steering straight. Once the car is stable and slower, brake gently and pull completely off the road.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 74, NJ p. 109, AZ p. 68)

prompt: You have regained control after a blowout, but you are still in a travel lane with no shoulder. A safe pull-off area is a short distance ahead. What should you do?
choices: Stop right away in your lane and change the tire
Stop in your lane, turn on your flashers, and wait for help
Drive slowly on the flat tire to the safe area, then stop completely off the road
Speed up so you get there before the tire comes apart
explanation: Driving slowly on a flat to reach a safe spot is better than stopping in traffic, even if it damages the rim. Make sure the car is off the road before you change the tire.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 67, TX p. 54, MT p. 87)

prompt: While driving, you hear a steady thumping from one of your wheels. What is the best thing to do?
choices: Pull safely off the road and check your tires
Turn up the radio and keep driving
Speed up to see if the noise stops
Brake hard to test the tire
explanation: A thumping sound can warn of a tire about to blow out or a loose wheel. Leave the road where it is safe and check the vehicle.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 65, AL p. 76)

prompt: Your car starts to skid on an icy road. What should you do with your right foot first?
choices: Brake hard
Press the gas to power out of the skid
Pump the brake quickly
Ease off the gas pedal
explanation: Gently take your foot off the accelerator and avoid hard braking. Braking during a skid can lock the wheels and make the skid worse.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 66, TX p. 54, FL p. 87)

prompt: When recovering from a skid, where should you look and steer?
choices: At the object you are trying to avoid
In the direction you want the car to go
In the opposite direction of where you want to go
Straight down at the hood
explanation: Look and steer where you want the car to go. Drivers tend to steer toward whatever they stare at.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 65, NJ p. 106, AZ p. 70)

prompt: On a wet road, the rear of your car begins sliding to the right. Which way should you steer?
choices: To the right
To the left
Keep the wheel perfectly straight
Sharply left, then brake
explanation: Steer in the direction the rear of the car is sliding (in the direction of the skid). If the rear slides right, steer right, without oversteering.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 65, NY p. 64, TX p. 54)

prompt: You correct a skid, and now the rear of the car starts sliding the other way. What should you do?
choices: Brake hard because the first correction failed
Hold the wheel still and wait
Steer smoothly in that new direction, correcting as many times as needed
Turn the wheel sharply and accelerate
explanation: A second, smaller skid in the opposite direction is common. Handle it the same way: steer toward where the rear is sliding, and keep correcting until the car is straight.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 65, NY p. 64, AZ p. 70)

prompt: Your car is front-wheel drive. How does that change the way you recover from a skid?
choices: Steer away from the direction of the skid
It does not change it: use the same method as in any car
Press the gas firmly to pull the car straight
Brake hard because front-wheel drive cars do not lock up
explanation: Handbooks teach the same skid recovery for front-, rear- and four-wheel drive cars: ease off the gas and steer where you want to go.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 106, NY p. 64)

prompt: In a car without ABS, you brake too hard. The wheels lock and the car keeps sliding forward no matter how you turn the wheel. What should you do?
choices: Push the brake pedal even harder
Turn the steering wheel farther
Shift into Park
Ease off the brake so the wheels roll again, then steer
explanation: Locked wheels cannot steer. Release enough brake pressure to let the wheels turn so steering returns, then reapply the brake more gently.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 66, MT p. 88)

prompt: Your car has anti-lock brakes (ABS). How should you brake in an emergency stop?
choices: Pump the pedal rapidly
Press lightly and release several times
Press the pedal firmly and keep steady pressure on it
Use only the parking brake
explanation: With ABS, press hard and hold the pedal down. The system pumps the brakes for you, so pumping the pedal yourself makes it less effective.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 65, MT p. 88, AZ p. 69)

prompt: During a hard stop, your ABS brake pedal pulses and makes a grinding noise. What should you do?
choices: Keep firm pressure on the pedal; this is normal
Let up on the pedal because the brakes are failing
Pump the pedal to stop the noise
Shift to neutral right away
explanation: Pulsing and mechanical noises mean the ABS is working. Keep pressing firmly and steer around hazards.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 65, MT p. 88)

prompt: You must stop quickly in a car without ABS. What is the best technique?
choices: Press as hard as you can and hold it no matter what
Brake gently and steer onto the shoulder
Shift to neutral and use the parking brake
Brake firmly without locking the wheels; if they lock, ease up and reapply
explanation: Without ABS, locked wheels skid and cannot steer. Apply strong pressure just short of locking; if the wheels lock, release briefly and brake again.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., MT p. 88, PA p. 65, NJ p. 110)

prompt: What is the main advantage of anti-lock brakes in an emergency?
choices: The car always stops in a shorter distance
You can keep steering while braking hard
You no longer need a safe following distance
The car cannot skid on ice
explanation: ABS keeps the wheels from locking, so you keep steering control during hard braking. It does not guarantee shorter stops on every surface or replace safe following distance.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 110, MT p. 88)

prompt: Your gas pedal sticks and the car keeps speeding up. What should you do?
choices: Shift to neutral, brake, and steer to a safe place off the road
Turn the key to Lock
Reach down and pull the pedal up with your hand
Keep the car in gear and drive on until the pedal frees itself
explanation: Shifting to neutral takes power away from the wheels. Then brake, steer off the road, and turn the engine off once you are stopped.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 110, PA p. 66, MT p. 87)

prompt: Your gas pedal is stuck, so you shift into neutral and the engine suddenly roars loudly. What does this mean?
choices: Something is broken, so shift back into Drive right away
The engine will stall, so turn the key to Lock
It is normal; the engine is no longer driving the wheels, so brake and pull off
The brakes have failed, so use the parking brake
explanation: In neutral, the racing engine is disconnected from the wheels. Brake, steer off the road, and turn the engine off once you are stopped.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 66, NJ p. 110)

prompt: Your right wheels drift off the pavement onto a soft shoulder. What should you do first?
choices: Jerk the wheel left to get back on the road
Hold the wheel firmly and ease off the gas
Brake hard to stop quickly
Speed up to climb back onto the pavement
explanation: Stay calm, grip the wheel, and take your foot off the gas. Do not jerk the wheel or brake hard.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 74, TX p. 55, PA p. 68)

prompt: Why is it dangerous to steer sharply back onto the road right after your wheels drop off the pavement edge?
choices: It will flatten your tires
It wears out the steering
It is illegal to drive on the shoulder
The car can whip across the road into oncoming traffic
explanation: A sharp turn to climb a pavement edge can make the car suddenly shoot across the lanes. Slow down first, then steer back gently.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 68, NJ p. 107, CA p. 74)

prompt: Your right wheels are on the shoulder below the pavement edge. You have eased off the gas and are straddling the edge. What should you do next?
choices: Turn back sharply while still at highway speed
Brake hard with two wheels on the soft shoulder
Slow down, check traffic behind you, signal, and steer gently back onto the road
Stop on the shoulder and wait for a tow truck
explanation: Once your speed is low and the lane is clear, ease the wheels back onto the pavement with a small steering movement. Hard braking with two wheels on a soft shoulder can cause a skid.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 68, TX p. 55, NY p. 65)

prompt: Your engine dies while you are driving. What should you expect and do?
choices: Steering and braking will be harder, so grip firmly, press the brake harder, and pull off the road
The brakes will no longer work at all, so use only the parking brake
The steering locks immediately, so let go of the wheel
Keep driving in neutral until the engine restarts itself
explanation: Without the engine, power steering and power brakes lose their assist, but they still work. Use extra effort to steer and brake, and get off the road.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., MT p. 87, NJ p. 109, AZ p. 69)

prompt: Your steering wheel suddenly stops responding when you turn it. What should you do?
choices: Brake hard to stop as fast as you can
Shift to a lower gear right away
Speed up to keep the car balanced
Ease off the gas, turn on your flashers, and brake very gently as the car slows
explanation: A sudden change in speed can throw the car out of control. Slow down gradually; once the car is slower, brake carefully to a stop.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 65, AL p. 76)

prompt: Your headlights suddenly go out at night. What should you try first?
choices: Stop immediately in your lane
Work the headlight and dimmer (high/low beam) switches
Keep driving and follow the car ahead
Turn off the engine and restart it
explanation: Flipping the headlight or dimmer switch may bring the lights back. If not, turn on parking lights, flashers or turn signals and pull off the road.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 69, NJ p. 109, MT p. 87)

prompt: Your headlights fail at night, and the switches do not bring them back. What should you do?
choices: Turn on your flashers, parking lights or turn signals and pull off the road as soon as it is safe
Keep driving slowly in the center of the road
Follow the taillights of another car to your destination
Stop where you are and turn off all lights
explanation: Other lights may still work and give you enough light to be seen and leave the road safely. Then call for help.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 65, NJ p. 109, AZ p. 69)

prompt: Your hood suddenly flies up and blocks your view. How can you see the road?
choices: Stick your head out the window while speeding up
Brake hard and stop in the lane
Look through the gap under the hood or out your side window
Turn on the windshield wipers
explanation: There is often a gap below the raised hood, and the side window gives another view. Use them to steer while you slow down.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 110, NY p. 66)

prompt: You see smoke coming from under the hood while driving. What should you do first?
choices: Keep driving to the nearest repair shop
Pull off the road and turn off the ignition
Open the hood while the engine runs to look
Speed up to blow the smoke away
explanation: Get off the road and shut off the ignition, which cuts electrical power. Most vehicle fires start in the electrical system.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 66, AZ p. 68, AL p. 77)

prompt: After stopping your car because of a fire, what is the top priority?
choices: Gather your belongings from the trunk
Stay inside with the windows closed
Try to drive to a gas station for help
Get everyone out and well away from the car, then call 911
explanation: People come first. Get everyone away from the car and call for help; fighting a car fire yourself is dangerous.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 108, NY p. 66, AZ p. 68)

prompt: Why should you never use water on a burning gasoline fire?
choices: Water makes the car battery explode
Water freezes on hot metal
The burning gasoline floats on water and spreads the flames
Water damages the paint
explanation: Gasoline floats on water, so water spreads the fire. If you use anything, use a fire extinguisher, and get away if the fire is not quickly controlled.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 68, AL p. 77)

prompt: Steam is pouring from under your hood. What should you do after pulling off and turning off the engine?
choices: Leave the radiator cap closed until the engine cools
Open the radiator cap right away to let steam out
Pour cold water on the hot engine
Restart the engine to run the fan
explanation: Steam usually means overheating. Opening a hot radiator cap can spray boiling coolant and cause severe burns; add coolant or water only after the engine cools.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 68, AL p. 77)

prompt: Your car stalls on railroad tracks and a train is coming. What should you do?
choices: Keep trying to start the engine
Stay inside with your seat belt on
Get out and try to push the car off
Get everyone out right away and move away from the tracks
explanation: Leave the vehicle immediately. A train cannot stop quickly, and your car is not worth your life.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 76, NJ p. 108, FL p. 87)

prompt: After leaving a car stalled on the tracks with a train approaching, which way should you go?
choices: Along the tracks in the same direction the train is going
Away from the tracks at an angle toward the direction the train is coming from
Straight back to the car to grab your things
Across the tracks in front of the train
explanation: When the train hits the car, debris is thrown forward in the train's direction of travel. Moving away at an angle toward the train keeps you out of that path.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 108, CA p. 76, FL p. 87, NY p. 66)

prompt: Your car is stuck on the tracks, everyone is out, and no train is in sight. Whom should you call?
choices: The emergency phone number on the blue sign at the crossing, and 911
A tow company only
Your insurance company first
No one, if you can push the car off later
explanation: Every public crossing has a blue Emergency Notification System sign with a railroad phone number. The railroad can warn or stop trains headed for the crossing.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 24, AK p. 64, CA p. 76)

prompt: You are stalled on a crossing, and the warning lights start flashing, but you cannot see a train yet. What should you do?
choices: Keep trying to restart the engine until you see the train
Wait in the car until you hear the horn
Get out immediately, because a train may arrive within seconds
Push the car off the tracks yourself
explanation: Flashing lights mean a train is on its way and may arrive in seconds. Leave the car right away and move well clear of the tracks.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 87, AK p. 64, CA p. 76)

prompt: Your car goes into deep water and is still floating. What should you do?
choices: Wait for the car to sink before trying to leave
Unbuckle and escape through a window right away
Call 911 first and wait for rescuers
Open the door and swim out
explanation: A car floats only briefly. Unbuckle and get out through a window while you can; opening a door lets water rush in.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 66, FL p. 88, NJ p. 108)

prompt: Your car with power windows has just plunged into water. When should you try to open the windows?
choices: After the car fills with water
Once you have called for help
Only after the car touches the bottom
Immediately, before the electrical system shorts out
explanation: Power windows may stop working once water reaches the electrical system, so open them right away. If they will not open, try to break a side window.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 108, FL p. 88)

prompt: Your car has sunk before you could get out. Where is an air pocket most likely to form?
choices: Under the dashboard
Near the floor in front
Near the roof at the back of the car
Inside the trunk
explanation: Most cars have the engine in front and sink nose first, pushing air toward the rear near the roof. Take a breath there, then escape through a window.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 108, NY p. 66, AL p. 77)

prompt: Your car plunges into a lake. When should you call 911?
choices: After you are out of the vehicle
Before unbuckling, so help is on the way
While waiting for the car to sink
Instead of trying to escape
explanation: The car may float for only a short time. Spend those seconds getting out; call for help once you are safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 88)

prompt: To avoid a possible collision, which three actions can a driver take?
choices: Honk, flash your lights, or wave
Stop, back up, or turn off the engine
Brake hard, shift to neutral, or turn off the lights
Stop, turn (steer away), or speed up
explanation: Depending on the situation, you may avoid a crash by stopping, steering away, or speeding up out of danger.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 110, MT p. 88)

prompt: At highway speed, a hazard suddenly appears close ahead, and the lane beside you is clear. Which is often quickest to avoid it?
choices: Braking to a complete stop
Steering around it
Shifting into neutral
Sounding the horn and holding your course
explanation: In most cases you can turn the car faster than you can stop it. Grip the wheel with both hands and steer into the open space.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., MT p. 88, NJ p. 111)

prompt: A car is coming toward you in your lane on a two-lane road. What should you do?
choices: Slow down, move to the right, and sound your horn
Swerve into the left lane
Speed up and flash your high beams
Stop in your lane and wait
explanation: Slow, steer right, and warn the other driver with your horn (and lights at night). Escape to the right, even onto the shoulder.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 65, PA p. 68, AZ p. 69)

prompt: An oncoming car drifts into your lane. Why is swerving into the left lane a bad idea?
choices: It is always illegal to cross the center line
Your car cannot turn left at speed
The other driver may recover and move back into that same lane
The left lane is always slower
explanation: If the other driver corrects at the last moment, you would meet head-on in the left lane. Move right instead.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 68, NY p. 65, AL p. 76)

prompt: A crash cannot be avoided. Which is the safest thing to hit?
choices: A tree
Bushes or shrubs that will give way
A concrete wall
A utility pole
explanation: If you must hit something, choose an object that will give way and absorb energy, not something hard.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 111)

prompt: You cannot avoid hitting one of these. Which choice is likely to be least severe?
choices: A parked car
A vehicle coming straight at you
A stone wall
A vehicle ahead moving in the same direction as you
explanation: Hitting something moving the same way reduces the force of impact. A stopped object is worse, and a head-on crash with oncoming traffic is the worst.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 111)

prompt: If a crash is unavoidable, what kind of impact should you try for?
choices: A direct, square hit so the air bags work
A hit on the driver's side
A glancing blow instead of a head-on hit
A full-speed hit to get it over quickly
explanation: Steering even slightly away so you strike at an angle spreads out the crash energy and reduces injury. Avoid head-on impacts.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 111, MT p. 89)

prompt: When can speeding up be the best way to avoid a crash?
choices: When a vehicle is about to hit you from the side or behind and there is room ahead
Whenever a light turns yellow
When a pedestrian steps out in front of you
When the car ahead stops suddenly
explanation: If danger is coming from the side or rear and the space ahead is clear, accelerating can get you out of the way. Slow back down once you are clear.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 111, MT p. 89)

prompt: You are stopped and see in your mirror that a car is about to hit you from behind. How should you protect yourself?
choices: Lean forward toward the steering wheel
Unbuckle your seat belt so you can get out fast
Turn around in your seat to watch the car
Press your head against the head restraint and brace against the seat back
explanation: In a rear crash your body is thrown backward. Keeping your head against the head restraint helps prevent neck injury.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 111, MT p. 89)

prompt: Your car is about to be hit from the side. What should you do?
choices: Let go of the wheel and cover your face
Keep a firm grip on the wheel and be ready to steer and brake after impact
Unbuckle and lean toward the other side
Turn the engine off
explanation: Holding the wheel helps keep you in position, and you must be ready to control the car if it spins after the hit.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 112, MT p. 89)

prompt: Your car breaks down on the highway. What should you do?
choices: Pull as far off the road as possible and turn on your hazard flashers
Stop in your lane and wait for help
Leave your lights off to save the battery
Stop on the next curve where the road is wider
explanation: Get completely off the road if you can and turn on your flashers so other drivers can see you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 18, TX p. 54, NJ p. 107)

prompt: Where should you place warning triangles or flares when your car is broken down on the shoulder?
choices: In front of your vehicle only
On top of your vehicle
Behind your vehicle, facing approaching traffic
In the next lane over, beside your car
explanation: Warning devices go behind the car so approaching drivers get early warning and can slow down and move over.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 107, TX p. 54, MT p. 89)

prompt: Your car is losing power and you need to stop. Which place should you avoid stopping?
choices: A wide, straight shoulder
Just over the top of a hill or just around a curve
A parking lot
A highway exit ramp shoulder with good visibility
explanation: Drivers coming over a hill or around a curve may not see your car in time to avoid hitting it.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 18)

prompt: Your car broke down on a freeway shoulder and you must get out. Which is the safest way?
choices: Exit on the driver's side so you can reach the trunk quickly
Stand directly behind the car to wave traffic over
Walk along the edge of the travel lane to find help
Exit on the side away from traffic and stay out of the travel lanes
explanation: Get out on the side away from traffic. Standing behind the car can block your taillights and put you in the path of a crash.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 75, NJ p. 107, MT p. 89)

prompt: You are involved in a minor crash with only slight damage. Must you stop?
choices: No, only if someone is hurt
No, only if the police arrive
Yes, you must stop no matter how small the damage
No, only if the damage is serious
explanation: Drivers involved in any crash must stop. Leaving the scene is a hit-and-run and can carry severe penalties.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 77, CA p. 83, MT p. 89)

prompt: Someone is hurt in a crash you are involved in. What should you do?
choices: Call 911 right away
Drive the injured person home
Wait to see if they feel better
Leave and report it the next day
explanation: Get police and medical help right away whenever anyone is injured.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 83, FL p. 85, AZ p. 71)

prompt: When must the police be notified of a crash?
choices: Only when a car must be towed
Only when the other driver asks
Only when the crash was your fault
Whenever anyone is injured or killed
explanation: A crash with injury or death must always be reported to police. Many states also require a report for property damage; check your state's rules.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., MT p. 89, NY p. 77, TX p. 65)

prompt: After a crash, should you move an injured person?
choices: Yes, always move them into your car
No, unless they are in immediate danger, such as from fire
Yes, sit them up so they can breathe
Yes, carry them to the side of the road
explanation: Moving an injured person can make injuries worse. Move them only if they are in immediate danger, keeping the back and neck as straight as possible.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 77, MT p. 90)

prompt: Which information should drivers exchange after a crash?
choices: Name, address, driver license number, vehicle plate, and insurance details
Only first names and phone numbers
Only the insurance company's name
Nothing until a lawyer is present
explanation: Exchange full identifying details: name, address, license number, plate and vehicle information, and insurance company and policy number. Also note witnesses.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 77, AZ p. 71, MT p. 90)

prompt: You back into an unattended parked car and cannot find the owner. What should you do?
choices: Drive away if the damage looks small
Wait 10 minutes and then leave
Leave a note with your name and contact information and report it to police
Take a photo and leave without a note
explanation: Try to find the owner. If you cannot, securely attach a note with your name and how to reach you, and notify police.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 83, FL p. 85, MT p. 90)

prompt: After a minor crash with no injuries, both cars can still be driven but are blocking traffic. What is usually best?
choices: Leave the cars exactly where they are until police arrive
Move the cars out of the travel lanes to a safe spot, then exchange information
Stand in the lane to direct traffic around the cars
Drive home and call the other driver later
explanation: When no one is hurt and the cars are drivable, moving them out of traffic reduces the risk of a second crash. Do not leave the scene.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 83, AZ p. 71, FL p. 85)

prompt: After a crash, a power line has fallen across your car. What should you do?
choices: Get out and run to the nearest house
Try to push the wire off with your hand
Get out and wait right beside the car
Stay inside and warn others to stay away until help arrives
explanation: If wires touch the car, occupants should stay inside until help arrives, and others should not go near the wires.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 77, MT p. 89)

prompt: A crash victim is bleeding heavily. What is the best first aid while you wait for help?
choices: Give the person water to drink
Have the person stand up and walk to your car
Press firmly on the wound with a cloth or your hand
Leave it alone until paramedics arrive
explanation: Direct pressure on the wound can stop or slow even severe bleeding.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., MT p. 90)

prompt: Why is carbon monoxide from car exhaust so dangerous?
choices: It is a deadly gas you cannot see or smell
It always smells strongly of gasoline
It only affects people outside the car
It is harmless when the engine is warm
explanation: Carbon monoxide is colorless and odorless, so you will not notice it building up. It can kill.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 99, CA p. 77, NJ p. 50)

prompt: Which set of symptoms may signal carbon monoxide poisoning while driving?
choices: Sneezing and itchy eyes
Hunger and thirst
Sore muscles and a stiff neck
Headache, dizziness, nausea, and unusual tiredness or yawning
explanation: Headache, dizziness, nausea, drowsiness and yawning are common signs. If you notice them, get fresh air right away and have your exhaust system checked.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 77, PA p. 99, AL p. 75)

prompt: Which practice helps prevent carbon monoxide poisoning?
choices: Warm up the car in a closed garage on cold days
Never run the engine inside a garage, even with the door open
Keep all windows tightly closed while idling
Drive with the trunk or tailgate open
explanation: Idling in a garage or other enclosed space lets exhaust build up. An open trunk or tailgate can also pull exhaust into the car.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 50, CA p. 77, TX p. 74)

prompt: You are stranded in a snowstorm and run the engine for heat. What should you do to avoid carbon monoxide poisoning?
choices: Keep the tailpipe clear of snow and open a window slightly
Close every window tightly to keep the heat in
Run the engine nonstop all night
Pack snow around the back of the car for insulation
explanation: A tailpipe blocked by snow can force exhaust into the car. Run the engine only sometimes, with a window cracked open for fresh air.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NE p. 71, NJ p. 50)

prompt: A passenger becomes dizzy and confused, and you suspect carbon monoxide. What should you do?
choices: Turn up the heater and keep driving
Let them sleep it off in the car
Get them into fresh air right away and call 911
Give them coffee to wake them up
explanation: Fresh air is the cure for carbon monoxide exposure. Move the person to fresh air and call 911 for medical help.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 74, AL p. 75, AK p. 81)
